E. JURISDICTION AND VENUE
1.SUBJECT-MATTER JURISDICTION
Some of the more difficult questions about subject-matter jurisdiction affecting the class action reflect uncertainty whether Rule 23 is
a joinder device or a representative procedure. Within the joinder model, each absentee class member must satisfy jurisdictional and
venue requirements; within the representative model, only the named party is significant. As you study these questions, consider whether
the Court’s approach to the topic has changed over the years.
NOTES AND QUESTIONS
1. A class action based upon a federal question usually does not raise any special problems of subject-matter jurisdiction. A class action based
upon diversity, however, does raise two special questions: first, to which class members should the court look in determining whether there is diversity
of citizenship and, second, to which class members should the court look in calculating the jurisdictional amount?
2. In SUPREME TRIBE OF BEN-HUR v. CAUBLE, 255 U.S. 356, 41 S.Ct. 338, 65 L.Ed. 673 (1921), the Court held that determinations of
diversity of citizenship in class actions should be based on the citizenship of the named parties only. How does this rule apply to a class action brought
by a corporation or an unincorporated association?
3.In SNYDER v. HARRIS, 394 U.S. 332, 89 S.Ct. 1053, 22 L.Ed.2d 319 (1969), Snyder, a shareholder of Missouri Fidelity Union Trust Life
Insurance Co., brought suit in federal court against members of the company’s board of directors. Since the petitioner’s allegations showed that she
